The available data suggest that all three groups of pedestrians (normally sighted, visually impaired, and blind) have varying levels of accuracy and reliability when it comes to making street crossing decisions.

For normally sighted pedestrians, research indicates that they can make accurate and reliable street crossing decisions. However, when using auditory information only, there is a significant overestimation of the vehicular gap time.

In contrast, visually impaired pedestrians seem to perform similarly to normally sighted pedestrians under this condition. In fact, one study found that blind pedestrians performed significantly worse than either the normally sighted or visually impaired subjects under the hearing only condition.

This suggests that visually impaired individuals may need additional training or guidance to improve their detection ability and interpretation of vehicular gap times when making street crossing decisions.

It's essential to note that these findings have limitations, and further research is needed to fully understand the accuracy and reliability of pedestrian decision-making in different scenarios.
